text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--- Danish foreign minister Niels Helveg Petersen will face demands from parliamentary parties for a tougher policy on developmental aid for China when he returns from his official visit to China because of the human rights situation.

--- An accident on the Great Belt road-rail tunnel-bridge fixed link between the islands of Zealand and Funen caused the eighth death on the project, sparking criticism of safety. The rail section is due to open in June 1997, four years late, with the car suspension bridge expected to be completed a year later.

--- The international Hell's Angels biker gang has now increased its clubhouses in Denmark by one to a total of five, with a new base in Odense, central Denmark. Police fear the turf war between the Hell's Angels and rival group Bandidos will now spread to that part of Denmark.

--- Copenhagen authorities are to offer free AIDS tests to some 4,000 drug addicts in the capital. The tests will be carried out by mobile laboratories touring areas where the addicts are resident. The authorities estimate that about 10-15 percent of drug addicts are HIV-positive.

--- Denmark's central bank says in its latest quarterly report that the country's foreign debt continues to decrease. At end-1995 Danish foreign debt amounted to 266 billion crowns or 28 percent of GDP compared to 1991 when it was 40 percent, meaning that Danish foreign debt is now lower than that of Sweden, Finland, Spain and Ireland.

--- Danish communications minister Jan Troejborg is calling for the postal service to live up to its target of ensuring that 97 percent of all post reaches recipients within a day of posting. Only 93.3 percent of post reaches its destination on time now.

--- Denmark is to be joined by France and Germany to fight in the European Court for the right to go on using the name feta for one of its best selling cheese products with exports worth 1.5 billion crowns per annum. Greece claims it has the sole right to produce the cheese.
